# Didache Chapter 8 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Codex Hierosolymitanus (H), Didache 8

---

## Chapter 8

**1** Do not observe your fasts at the same time as the hypocrites — for they fast on the second and fifth days of the week. Instead, fast on the fourth day and on the Day of Preparation.

**2** Do not pray as the hypocrites do. Rather, pray as the Lord commanded in his Gospel:

> Our Father, who art in heaven,
> hallowed be thy name;
> thy kingdom come;
> thy will be done,
> as in heaven, so also on earth;
> give us today our daily bread;
> and forgive us our debt,
> as we also forgive our debtors;
> and lead us not into temptation,
> but deliver us from evil;
> for thine is the power and the glory forever.

**3** Pray this way three times each day.

---

### Council Notes

**On the Lord's Prayer — translation philosophy:** The Lord's Prayer is among the most sensitive translation decisions in all of Christian literature. SOPHIA adopts the traditional English liturgical rendering for the prayer body (matching the KJV/BCP tradition closely) because: (1) this is the form in which billions of Christians pray it; (2) the Didache itself is presenting a liturgical text meant to be used in worship; (3) the Greek closely matches Matthew 6:9-13, and our translation of the prayer should reflect this canonical relationship.

**On v.2 — "lead us not into temptation" vs. "do not bring us to the time of testing":** PNEUMA offers the more interpretively accurate "do not bring us to the time of testing" (πειρασμός = testing/trial, not merely personal temptation). However, SOPHIA retains the traditional "lead us not into temptation" as the recognized liturgical form, noting in commentary that πειρασμός has eschatological dimensions.

**On "debt" vs. "trespasses" vs. "sins":** The Didache uses ὀφείλημα (debt), matching Matthew 6:12. Luke 11:4 uses ἁμαρτία (sins). SOPHIA retains "debt" — the Matthean/Didache term — both for accuracy and because it preserves the economic metaphor of moral obligation.

**On the doxology ("for thine is the power and the glory forever"):** This is absent from Matthew's best manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) but present in the Didache and in the Byzantine tradition. This confirms the doxology was a liturgical addition in common use by c. 100 CE. SOPHIA retains it as it is part of the Didache text.

**On "Day of Preparation" (παρασκευή):** All agents agree. This is the technical term for Friday (day before Sabbath) — important to retain rather than translating as simply "Friday."
